notes.claim: BS 7671 itself has no diversity table; Regulation 311.1 asks the designer to assess maximum demand (of the whole installation or a part of it), and the On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.
Maximum demand is the largest current an installation draws at any one time, which is why the supply and every submain are sized from it.
Diversity is common-sense guidance from the On-Site Guide's Appendix A, not a rule; the slides give 66% for a domestic lighting circuit as the example.

Sources differ on where diversity is applied: the course slides apply 66% to the Ib of a lighting circuit, while a training provider says diversity applies to the aggregate demand at the origin, not to individual circuits.
notes.contested: Dan's slides apply diversity to the design current of a lighting circuit; Total Skills says to size each circuit on its full design current and apply diversity only to the aggregate demand.

notes.claim: The assignment asks for loads to be balanced across circuits (question 1b), links this to the maximum-demand question 10, and points to Section 3 of The Electrical Installation Guide for demand and diversity factors.
Balanced fundamental currents leave no current in the neutral (a balanced motor load needs no neutral), and an IET forum contributor suggests spreading demand about one third to each phase.
For the EV charge points the guide says load management may be considered to reduce maximum demand but is not compulsory, and Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment be taken into account.

The lighting drawing's key gives each fitting's wattage (for example 4 × 36 W modular fluorescent, 58 W twin fluorescent, 70 W column luminaires), to be recounted by hand; the power drawing marks 63 A isolators and 2 × 32 A EV points.

Dan's Level 4 specification asks him to state the purpose of diversity factors and to determine the maximum demand of an installation after diversity, covering the application of the IET On-Site Guide.
The slides give the purpose of diversity as designing with 'common sense' rather than the maximum demand, which keeps cable sizes smaller and costs lower (the points for the Section B answer).

For small shops, stores, offices and business premises the On-Site Guide's diversity table gives: lighting 90% of total current demand; heating and power 100% of the largest appliance plus 75% of the remaining appliances; motors (not lifts) 100% of the largest motor plus 80% of the second and 60% of the rest; socket-outlets 100% of the largest point plus 70% of every other point; standard final-circuit arrangements 100% of the largest circuit plus 50% of every other. A showroom is taken to fit this column, which is the course's own assumption.

Sources differ on the small-shop socket-outlet allowance: the table as printed by an electrician's page gives 70% of every other point, an older book (16th Edition era) gives 75%, and the table is numbered A2, H2 or 1B depending on the source and edition, so the lesson names the rule and sends him to his own copy for the figure.
notes.contested: One page prints 100% of the largest point plus 70% of every other point for small shops; an older book prints 100%X + 75%(Y+Z). Table numbering also differs between sources.

notes.claim: For electric vehicle charging: the original 2018 text allowed no diversity on a final circuit with more than one charging point and diversity on a dedicated distribution circuit only with load control; Amendment 1 replaced that with Regulation 722.311.201, which lets load curtailment be taken into account; the IEC wording sets the diversity factor at 1 unless a load management system is used, and the Schneider guide takes the utilisation factor as 1.

Whether Amendment 1 allows any diversity on EV charging is argued on the IET forum: one contributor says BS 7671 does not prohibit it, another that without load management it is still zero diversity; the lesson takes none without load management.
notes.contested: gkenyon (IET EngX): BS 7671 does not prohibit diversity for EV charging points. pww235: in the absence of a load management system it is still zero diversity.

notes.claim: Where diversity is applied is argued: the On-Site Guide table is applied by type of final circuit; the Schneider guide applies its simultaneity factor to a group of loads fed from a distribution board and says the designer is responsible for it; an IET webinar answer says for a single circuit's design current diversity might only rarely be appropriate; an older book says distribution boards must carry their total connected load; the Schneider guide also advises simultaneity factors close to unity when the circuits are mainly lighting.
notes.contested: Sources disagree on whether diversity belongs on each circuit's design current (the slides' 66% example), on a group of circuits at a board, or only on the aggregate at the origin.

notes.claim: Maximum demand is the largest current normally carried by circuits, switches and protective devices; the IET describes it as the sum of the connected loads multiplied by a factor for diversity, and accepts that with diversity applied it may occasionally be exceeded; a forum contributor says the 'official' maximum demand is the rating of the supply fuse.
notes.contested: IET webinar: maximum demand is the connected load multiplied by a diversity factor. An IET EngX contributor: the official maximum demand is the supply fuse rating. The lesson uses the designer's assessment (Regulation 311.1) and says so.

notes.claim: A page on diversity warns that the On-Site Guide's table is aimed at small domestic and similar installations and that commercial and industrial maximum demand may need load measurements or building-services standards, so a showroom with an 11 kW motor and EV points rests on informed assumptions, as question 10 asks.

For a lighting load from a key wattage: the tube power marked on a fluorescent lamp excludes the ballast, 25% of Pn may be used when no ballast loss is given, and cos φ is 0.96 with an electronic ballast; an older book gives current = lamp power x 1.8 / voltage for discharge lighting when the power factor is not below 0.85; each lampholder counts at least 100 W; a separated LED driver's power is not in the module's marked watts, and makers' datasheets for 36 W LED panels state power factors of 0.97 and 0.95.

To balance a three-phase board, single-phase circuits are spread about equally over L1, L2 and L3 because unbalanced line currents do not cancel in the neutral; the most heavily loaded phase fixes the supply requirement; and with a perfect balance the three-phase line current is the total single-phase current divided by three, as an older book works it. Dan's guide asks for a schedule of circuits and his slides say a balanced three-phase load carries no neutral current.

The motor is the only motor on the case, so in the small-shop column it counts at 100% of its full-load current (23.08 A); the Schneider guide instead applies a utilisation factor of about 0.75 to motors in an industrial installation, a different method that the lesson names but does not use.
notes.contested: On-Site Guide small-shop column: 100% of the largest motor. Schneider guide: utilisation factor ku about 0.75 for motors in industrial installations, plus a separate simultaneity factor.

notes.claim: The power drawing's key marks twin switched sockets, 20 A DP switches, a 32 A rotary isolator, 63 A TPN isolators and EV points of 2 x 32 A each, with each charging point having two outlets; the equipment behind the 20 A and 32 A switches is not stated, so the loads there are practice values.

The lighting drawing's key adds a 26 W LED fitting, a wall spot light of 2 x 35 W, an 18 W walkway bollard and an 18 W IP65 bulkhead to the fluorescent and column fittings already noted; the lamp types behind the spot and column fittings are not stated.
